subsystem: Guardrails A — tool-definition integrity (anti rug-pull) + pre-call policy engine
summary: Both halves collapse into one comparison evaluated inside a predicate that already exists. Integrity is not a state machine you drive — it is `approved_hash === def_hash`, one extra AND term inside the settled `isExposed`, so a server that mutates a tool at 03:00 is quarantined by arithmetic the instant the new hash lands, with no watcher, no background job and no transition code. Policy is not a language — it is a first-match scan over an ordered in-memory array of Postgres rows, called from the single `callTool` site through an injected synchronous gate, so there is no parser, no sandbox, no cache to invalidate. The engine writes facts (`tool_embedding.def_hash`), the operator writes opinions (`server_item_override.review_state/approved_hash`), and `changed` is derived from the disagreement — never stored, so it cannot go stale. Grants stay default-deny and mandatory; policy is default-allow and purely subtractive, which is what keeps it 450 lines instead of 2000. The asymmetry that decides every error-surface question: for integrity the adversary is upstream, so the client learns nothing (`Tool not found`, byte-identical); for policy the adversary is nobody — the caller is a legitimate principal — so the client learns exactly what the operator chose to tell it.
phase: P2 (+1.0w) and P3 (+1.0w). Total +2.0 dev-weeks → 14.5. P2 "scope + visibility invariant" takes the hash module, the four columns, the `isExposed` AND term, the `policy_rule` table, `evaluate`, and the gate seam — because both are terms in the same two predicates (`isExposed`, `callTool`) and retrofitting a gate into a dispatch path later is exactly the shape of mcphub's afcc72f CVE. The P2 invariant suite grows by ~12 cases (quarantined ≡ nonexistent byte-for-byte; every path reaching `dispatch` passed the gate; fail-closed arg ops). P3 "operator UI" takes the review queue, the pointer-flattened diff, the rule editor with sentence rendering, and the explain drawer — ~700 LOC of the 2050, and the half that decides whether anyone keeps the feature on.

decisions.decision: Canonicalisation is recursive key-sort + `JSON.stringify`, with NFC applied to string VALUES only (never to keys), SHA-256 hex. No RFC 8785 library, no canonicalisation dependency.
decisions.rationale: We only ever compare our own hashes to our own hashes, so we need determinism, not interoperability — and V8's `JSON.stringify` is already deterministic for numbers, strings and escapes; the only missing piece is key order, which is 12 lines. NFC on values folds encoder churn that renders identically; NFKC is refused because it folds ligatures and full-width forms, which DO change rendering and are a known obfuscation vector; keys are left raw so a homoglyph property name is a change, not a fold.
decisions.cost: If we ever need to compare a hash with an external tool, we must swap in real JCS. Ceiling marked in the module header: `ponytail: determinism-only, not RFC 8785; swap to canonicalize@2 if a hash ever crosses a process boundary we do not own.`
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub has no definition hash at all — a tool's description can change silently between calls and nothing notices. The naive version is `sha256(JSON.stringify(tool))`, which is useless the first time a server swaps its JSON encoder and reorders keys; ours is three extra lines and immune to that.

decisions.decision: Engine-written facts (`def_hash`, `schema_hash`, `defect`, `def_seen_at`) go in `tool_embedding` next to `input_schema`. Operator-written opinions (`review_state`, `approved_hash`, `approved_by`, `approved_at`) go in the existing `server_item_override`. `changed` is DERIVED as `review_state='approved' AND approved_hash <> def_hash` and is never stored.
decisions.rationale: The settled column-vs-jsonb rule gives both answers directly: these are values Postgres must filter on (`isExposed`) AND values a concurrent writer (an operator clicking approve) edits independently of its siblings (the engine rewriting `input_schema`), so each gets its own column in the table its own writer owns. Deriving `changed` deletes the entire transition layer — there is no watcher to run, no window where the engine writes a new hash and forgets to flip a status, and no re-quarantine pass to schedule.
decisions.cost: The review queue needs a join between `tool_embedding` and `server_item_override` instead of one indexed scan. Both are keyed `(server_id, kind, item_name)`, the catalog is hundreds to low thousands of rows, and the in-memory catalog already carries both sides, so the join happens once per queue page, never on the hot path.
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub has neither table concept — approval does not exist. The naive version is a `status` enum column that a background differ maintains, which needs a job, a lock, and an answer for what happens when the job is down; ours needs none of that because the comparison is free at read time.

decisions.decision: Trust-on-first-use, but folded into the install confirmation. Items discovered on a server that has NEVER been enabled are written `approved` with `approved_hash = def_hash` and `approved_by = <the principal enabling it>` in the SAME transaction as `servers.enabled = true`. Items that appear later on an already-enabled server arrive `unreviewed`. Setting: `guardrails.newItemsOnEnabledServer: 'quarantine' | 'approve'`, default `quarantine`; plus `guardrails.integrity: 'enforce' | 'observe' | 'off'`, default `enforce`.
decisions.rationale: Block-by-default and TOFU converge if you notice that at install time the reviewer is already present, in the UI, looking at the screen — the Add-Server flow discovers the catalog with admin credentials (settled) before enabling, so its last step renders every tool with its token cost and annotations, and 'Enable server' IS the approve click. Nobody feels blocked, nothing is blessed without an attributed human action, and the named attack (approved benign, mutated later) is still fully covered because later mutations are exactly what the hash catches.
decisions.cost: A new tool shipped by an existing server does not appear until someone reviews it, which will surprise people once. Mitigated by the settled SSE `changed` frame, a count badge in the console header, and the item rendering greyed with a Review affordance rather than vanishing from the UI. `observe` exists so a team can roll the feature out without breaking their agents on day one; the default is `enforce` because a guardrail that ships off is theatre.

decisions.decision: A quarantined, rejected, defective or disabled item is byte-identical to a nonexistent one: `isExposed` returns false, `resolveTool` throws the single `Tool not found: ${name}` from the one existing construction site. A policy DENY is the opposite — the tool stays listed and the client gets a distinguishable JSON-RPC `-32003` `Blocked by policy` plus the rule's operator-authored `note`.
decisions.rationale: For integrity the adversary is the upstream server, and a distinguishable 'quarantined pending review' error tells them the tool exists, that we noticed their mutation, and when to stop — worse, it turns the calling model into the attacker's advocate ('ask your admin to approve tool X'). For policy the adversary is nobody: the caller already passed grant and group checks, the rule was written by our own operator, and the useful outcome is the model stopping its retry loop and telling the human why.
decisions.cost: A model holding a cached tool list gets a bare `Tool not found` mid-run. We emit `notifications/tools/list_changed` so a conforming client re-lists; we accept the confusion for non-conforming ones. The `note` string enters the model's context, so it is `varchar(200)`, text-only, never rendered as markdown, and writable only by admins — who could write an `allow` rule anyway, so it is no escalation.
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub got the hidden-vs-missing equivalence right (`ToolUnavailableError`) and we reproduce it exactly rather than inventing a second error path; the naive version adds a helpful 'this tool is quarantined' message and hands the attacker an oracle.

decisions.decision: At cache time, reject and mark `defect` for: any `$ref` that is not a local `#/...` pointer, schema nesting deeper than 64, canonical form larger than 256 KiB, or a canonicalisation throw. A defective item is never exposed in ANY integrity mode, including `off`.
decisions.rationale: An external `$ref` is a hash-invisible mutation channel — the schema text stays constant while its meaning changes on someone else's server — and dereferencing it at hash time would put network I/O and SSRF surface inside a hash function, which is unacceptable; refusing it costs 10 lines. Depth and size caps are ordinary trust-boundary validation: 4 MB of `[[[[…` will blow the stack in both the canonicaliser and the ref-walker, and no real tool schema is 10 levels deep.
decisions.cost: An OpenAPI-bridged server that legitimately uses an external `$ref` cannot be exposed. That is correct — the bridge deliberately does not dereference, so we cannot see what the model will be told. `integrity: 'off'` turns off REVIEW, not VALIDATION, and the Settings copy says so.

decisions.decision: The rule model is a table of ordered rows in Postgres, evaluated FIRST-MATCH on `(seq ASC, id ASC)`, with an implicit final `allow`. Reject an expression language; reject a single zod-validated JSON document.
decisions.rationale: An expression language needs a parser, a sandbox, an evaluation timeout and a security review of its own, cannot be indexed, diffed or per-rule audited, and no operator can predict its outcome — yes, a rule language that needs its own parser is almost certainly the wrong answer, and it is here. A single JSON document is one row edited by concurrent writers, i.e. mcphub's whole-file-rewrite lost-update bug reintroduced, and it loses per-rule attribution. First-match on an operator-ordered list is the one model every operator has already internalised from firewall and IAM ACLs: read top to bottom, stop at the first hit, put exceptions above the broad rule.
decisions.cost: Default-allow means the policy table cannot be the authorization layer — but it must not be: grants and group selection are already default-deny and mandatory, and policy is purely subtractive on top. A team that wants default-deny inside policy writes ONE row at `seq=9999`, `subject any / name '*' / deny`. Most-specific-wins was rejected because specificity across four orthogonal dimensions is a partial order needing tiebreak rules nobody can predict; deny-overrides was rejected because it cannot express an exception.
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub has no pre-call policy at all — the only lever is disabling a tool globally. The naive version is a per-tool allow-list column, which cannot express argument constraints, cannot express require_approval, and cannot express a temporary org-wide block.

decisions.decision: Seven argument ops: `present`, `absent`, `equals`, `oneOf`, `prefix`, `pathUnder`, `maxLen`. No regex, no boolean combinators, no general predicate. Constraints on one rule are ANDed; missing path or wrong type FAILS the constraint. Constraints are forbidden on `deny` rules (DB CHECK), so `else_effect` (default `deny`) is unambiguous.
decisions.rationale: Operator-supplied regex on the hot path is a ReDoS surface against attacker-influenced arguments, and more importantly operators write regexes that they believe are security controls and are not (`^/tmp/` happily passes `/tmp/../etc/passwd`) — the honest answer is to ship the op they actually mean, and `node:path/posix` already implements it in five lines. A general predicate language is a trap for the same reason as D6 plus one more: it makes the hot path's worst case unbounded. Fail-closed on a missing or wrongly-typed path is the detail that decides whether the feature is real — `{"path": ["/tmp","/etc"]}` must not slip past a string op.
decisions.cost: `pathUnder` is LEXICAL: it normalises, rejects `..`, NUL and backslash, and requires an absolute path (a relative one's meaning depends on an upstream cwd we cannot see, so it is unverifiable → deny). A symlink under `/tmp` pointing at `/etc` defeats it, and operators will assume otherwise. Marked in the code and in the UI helper text: `ponytail: lexical containment only; symlink resolution is the upstream server's job, not the gateway's.`

decisions.decision: Core takes an injected SYNCHRONOUS `PolicyGate` in its constructor, exactly like the settled `TransportFactory`, and calls it between `resolveTool` and `dispatch`. Core contains zero policy semantics, zero rule types beyond the result union, zero storage. `resolveTool` returns a branded `ResolvedTool` carrying a module-private symbol, and `dispatch` accepts nothing else.
decisions.rationale: This bends 'core makes no authz decision' by exactly one hair — core holds a reference to a decider it cannot implement — and buys the thing that matters most: ONE call site, the same reason `isExposed` is one predicate. The alternative (server calls `resolveTool`, evaluates, then calls `dispatch`) is purer but creates a second place that must remember to call the gate, which is precisely the class of bug afcc72f was. The brand makes a bypass a compile error and a runtime error simultaneously.
decisions.cost: Synchronous means no future async policy source (OPA, an external AS) without an API break, and it forces the snapshot design rather than allowing a lazy DB read. Both are deliberate: an await on the hot path of every tool call is not acceptable, and forcing the cache up front is why there is no invalidation bug to have. The most likely real bypass is Smart Routing's `call_tool` meta-tool dispatching internally — it MUST re-enter `Engine.callTool`, and the brand plus an invariant test enforce it.

decisions.decision: MCP tool annotations (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `openWorldHint`, `idempotentHint`) NEVER drive a runtime policy decision. They are included in `def_hash` and `schema_hash`, displayed and sorted on in the review queue, and used at AUTHORING time to seed a suggested starter ruleset the operator edits and saves as ordinary rows.
decisions.rationale: The spec says annotations are untrusted unless the server is trusted, and the trusted case is precisely the case where you do not need them — on a server you wrote, you can name your own tools; on one you did not, letting a rule key off `readOnlyHint` lets the server choose its own policy class by setting `readOnlyHint: true` on `rm -rf`. The replacement is that annotations are a REVIEWED FACT: flipping `destructiveHint` after approval changes the hash and quarantines the tool, which is strictly stronger than a runtime default would have been.
decisions.cost: No `annotation:` selector in the rule model, so 'deny all destructive tools for viewers' must be written as names or patterns. The starter-ruleset generator (a pure function over the discovered catalog, rendered as editable draft rows in the install flow) recovers most of the ergonomics for zero runtime trust.
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub ignores annotations entirely. The naive version is `if (tool.annotations?.destructiveHint) requireApproval()`, which is a policy engine the upstream server gets to program.

decisions.decision: Fail CLOSED at boot (initial rule load fails → MCP endpoints return 503, `/healthz` reports `ready:false`, non-zero exit if `MCPR_STRICT_BOOT`), fail STALE at refresh (keep the last good snapshot, red console banner, `mcprouter_policy_snapshot_age_seconds` gauge, `mcprouter_policy_reload_failures_total` counter). Never fail open. The gate never guards the console's own API.
decisions.rationale: There is no traffic to break at boot and a gateway serving without its policy is the exact incident, so refusing to start is free; once serving, hard-failing every call because a reload hiccuped is a worse outcome than a snapshot that is seconds stale and visibly flagged. The last clause is the lockout escape hatch: an admin who writes `deny *` at `seq 0` can still reach `/api/policy/rules` to delete it, so no `MCPR_POLICY_DISABLE` env bypass needs to exist — and therefore cannot be abused.
decisions.cost: A successful reload returning zero rows is honoured as a real empty ruleset (an operator deleting their last rule must work), so we cannot distinguish that from a catastrophic truncation. We accept it rather than adding a heuristic; the write path is audited and the console shows the rule count, which is the human-scale detection.

interfaces.name: canonical / defHashes / externalRefs
interfaces.notes: ~55 lines. Whitespace is NOT stripped or collapsed: a description whose trailing whitespace changed IS a changed description, and 200 newlines followed by injected text is the classic hiding place. Resource CONTENTS are never hashed (they change by design); only the descriptor. NFC does not defend against Cyrillic homoglyphs — that is the content-labelling agent's confusable check, explicitly handed off. Runnable check: a `demo()` asserting (a) key reorder → same hash, (b) NFD↔NFC description → same hash, (c) one added schema property → different hash, (d) full-width `ｒｍ` vs `rm` → different hash, (e) 200-deep array → DefectError('too_deep').

interfaces.name: tool_embedding — guardrail columns
interfaces.notes: Engine-written, at cache time, inside the settled generation guard — the hash write RIDES INSIDE the generation + client-identity check, it is not a second write beside it, or a slow discover from generation N could launder a stale definition over a fresh one. The cache upsert is `... WHERE def_hash IS DISTINCT FROM $new`, so a flapping server that reconnects every 30s with identical definitions produces zero writes, zero audit rows and zero SSE frames. `defSeenAt` only moves when the hash moves.

interfaces.name: server_item_override — review columns + the state machine as a CHECK
interfaces.notes: Stored states: unreviewed | approved | rejected. `changed` is DERIVED (`approved` AND `approved_hash <> def_hash`) — four observable states, three stored, zero transitions to schedule, and no window where a hash lands and a status column lags. `rejected` is kept distinct from `enabled=false` because the reasons differ (malicious vs merely noisy) and the UI badge differs; there is no precedence ambiguity because `isExposed` ANDs both. The override row SURVIVES an item disappearing from upstream: if it returns with the same definition the old approval still matches (no re-review); if it returns changed it quarantines. Disappear/reappear is therefore not an exploit.

interfaces.name: isExposed — the one predicate, with the integrity term
interfaces.notes: ONE added conjunct. `listTools = filter(isExposed).map(project)`; `resolveTool` consults the same predicate and throws the settled `Tool not found: ${name}` from the one existing construction site. Quarantined, rejected, defective, disabled, out-of-group, server-down and nonexistent are therefore byte-identical to the client by construction, not by discipline. Invariant test (P2): for every reason-to-hide, capture the serialised JSON-RPC error and assert byte equality against the nonexistent-tool case.

interfaces.name: Partial-discovery and stale-catalog rules
interfaces.notes: This is the highest-value 12 lines in A1 and the one an implementer would otherwise get wrong. The generation + client-identity check is the settled mcphub-derived guard; the point here is that the hash write must be INSIDE it. `listSafely` returns `{ok:false}` for a thrown or timed-out list, never an empty array.

interfaces.name: policy_rule
interfaces.sketch:
export const policyEffect  = pgEnum('policy_effect',  ['allow', 'deny', 'require_approval']);
export const policySubject = pgEnum('policy_subject', ['any', 'role', 'user', 'api_key']);

export const policyRule = pgTable('policy_rule', {
  id:          uuid('id').primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
  seq:         integer('seq').notNull(),                  // operator-visible order; UI rewrites all on reorder
  enabled:     boolean('enabled').notNull().default(true),
  subjectKind: policySubject('subject_kind').notNull().default('any'),
  subjectId:   text('subject_id'),                        // role name | user.id | betterAuth apiKey.id
  serverSlug:  text('server_slug'),                       // null = any server
  itemKind:    text('item_kind').$type<'tool'|'prompt'|'resource'|'any'>().notNull().default('tool'),
  namePattern: text('name_pattern').notNull().default('*'),// BARE name; literal text + '*' only
  effect:      policyEffect('effect').notNull(),
  elseEffect:  policyEffect('else_effect').notNull().default('deny'),  // when args fail
  args:        jsonb('args').$type<ArgConstraint[]>().notNull().default([]),
  note:        varchar('note', { length: 200 }),          // SHOWN TO THE CLIENT on a non-allow
  createdBy:   text('created_by').notNull(),
  createdAt:   timestamp('created_at', { withTimezone: true }).notNull().defaultNow(),
  updatedAt:   timestamp('updated_at', { withTimezone: true }).notNull().defaultNow(),
}, (t) => [
  index('policy_rule_order_idx').on(t.seq, t.id),
  check('subject_id_iff_kind', sql`(${t.subjectKind} = 'any') = (${t.subjectId} IS NULL)`),
  check('no_args_on_deny',     sql`${t.effect} <> 'deny' OR jsonb_array_length(${t.args}) = 0`),
]);
interfaces.notes: Rows, not a document: each is independently editable (no lost-update rewrite), independently audited (`audit_event` with before/after), and diffable in a PR if someone exports them. `args` is jsonb by the settled rule — one owner reads and writes it as a whole object and Postgres never filters inside it. Total order is `(seq, id)`; the editor always rewrites the whole list as `seq = index * 10` on reorder so seqs stay distinct in practice, and the explain output prints the effective order so any ambiguity is visible rather than mysterious.

interfaces.name: ArgConstraint + PolicyRule zod
interfaces.sketch:
const Ptr = z.string().max(200).regex(/^(\/(?:[^~/]|~[01])*)*$/, 'RFC 6901 JSON pointer');
const Str = z.string().max(512);

export const ArgConstraint = z.discriminatedUnion('op', [
  z.object({ op: z.literal('present'),   ptr: Ptr }),
  z.object({ op: z.literal('absent'),    ptr: Ptr }),
  z.object({ op: z.literal('equals'),    ptr: Ptr, value: Str }),
  z.object({ op: z.literal('oneOf'),     ptr: Ptr, values: z.array(Str).min(1).max(64) }),
  z.object({ op: z.literal('prefix'),    ptr: Ptr, value: Str }),   // STRING prefix. Not a path check.
  z.object({ op: z.literal('pathUnder'), ptr: Ptr, value: Str }),   // POSIX containment, lexical
  z.object({ op: z.literal('maxLen'),    ptr: Ptr, n: z.int().min(0).max(1_000_000) }),
]);
export type ArgConstraint = z.infer<typeof ArgConstraint>;

export const PolicyRuleInput = z.object({
  seq: z.int().min(0).max(1_000_000),
  enabled: z.boolean().default(true),
  subjectKind: z.enum(['any','role','user','api_key']).default('any'),
  subjectId: z.string().max(128).nullable().default(null),
  serverSlug: z.string().regex(/^[a-z0-9]([a-z0-9-]{0,62}[a-z0-9])?$/).nullable().default(null),
  itemKind: z.enum(['tool','prompt','resource','any']).default('tool'),
  namePattern: z.string().max(128).regex(/^[A-Za-z0-9_*.\-]+$/).default('*'),
  effect: z.enum(['allow','deny','require_approval']),
  elseEffect: z.enum(['allow','deny','require_approval']).default('deny'),
  args: z.array(ArgConstraint).max(16).default([]),
  note: z.string().max(200).nullable().default(null),
})
.refine((r) => (r.subjectKind === 'any') === (r.subjectId === null), 'subjectId iff a narrow subject')
.refine((r) => r.effect !== 'deny' || r.args.length === 0, 'constraints are not allowed on a deny rule')
.refine((r) => r.subjectKind !== 'role' || ['viewer','operator','admin'].includes(r.subjectId!), 'unknown role');
interfaces.notes: REFUSED ops: `matches` (regex) — ReDoS on the hot path against attacker-influenced args, and operators write regexes they believe are security controls and are not; `jsonSchema` — a schema inside a policy is a second untrusted schema evaluator; anything boolean (`and`/`or`/`not`) — that is the first step to the expression language, and first-match already gives you OR by writing a second rule above. Constraints on one rule are ANDed. Note the `namePattern` charset excludes the `__` namespace separator path entirely: patterns match BARE names, because `serverSlug` already carries the server.

interfaces.name: evaluate + Explain
interfaces.notes: `considered` is only allocated when `trace` is true, so the hot path allocates one object. Cold cost with 200 rules is a linear scan of cheap string compares — microseconds — so there is NO per-principal or per-tool memo: a memo keyed on (principal, tool) is unsound the moment args matter, and one keyed on args is unbounded. The rule array IS the cache.

interfaces.name: argsOk + pathUnder + ptrGet + globMatch
interfaces.kind: core of the arg constraints — same module
interfaces.notes: ~55 lines total, all seven ops. `~1` must be replaced before `~0` (RFC 6901 order) — the sketch does. Runnable check: an assert-based `demo()` covering `/tmp/../etc/passwd` → false, `/tmp` → true, `/tmpfoo` → false, array value under a string op → false, missing ptr under `equals` → false, `/constructor/prototype` → undefined, `a*b*c` glob against `aXbYc` and `abc`.

interfaces.name: PolicyGate — the core seam
interfaces.notes: The bend in 'core makes no authz decision', stated exactly: core holds a reference to a decider it cannot implement, and core still contains zero policy semantics, zero rule types beyond the result union, zero storage, and zero HTTP. The `RESOLVED` symbol is module-private, so `dispatch` is unreachable without passing through `resolveTool` + gate — a bypass is a compile error AND a runtime error. Smart Routing's `call_tool` meta-tool MUST re-enter `Engine.callTool`; mcphub intercepts meta-tools at the top of its call handler, and that is the single likeliest bypass in this codebase. P2 invariant test: spy on `dispatch` and assert every invocation in the suite was preceded by a gate call with a matching (server, bare).

interfaces.name: Route table
interfaces.sketch:
GET    /api/review?state=changed|unreviewed|defect&server=<slug>   operator  queue (joined view)
GET    /api/review/:slug/:kind/:name/diff                          operator  approved vs current
POST   /api/review/approve   {items:[{slug,kind,name,defHash}]}    operator  see TOCTOU note
POST   /api/review/approve   {slug, all:true, defHashes:{...}}     operator  bulk, per-server
POST   /api/review/reject    {items:[...]}                         operator  review_state='rejected'
PATCH  /api/servers/:slug    {trust:'reviewed'|'trusted'}          admin     auto-approve on change

GET    /api/policy/rules                                           admin     ordered
POST   /api/policy/rules             (PolicyRuleInput)             admin
PATCH  /api/policy/rules/:id         (PolicyRuleInput.partial())   admin
DELETE /api/policy/rules/:id                                       admin
POST   /api/policy/reorder   {ids:[...]}                           admin     rewrites seq = idx*10
POST   /api/policy/explain   {subject, slug, kind, name, args}     admin     evaluate(..., trace:true)

// TOCTOU: approve is `UPDATE ... SET approved_hash = e.def_hash ... WHERE e.def_hash = $seenHash`.
// If the definition moved between render and click -> 0 rows -> 409 + the NEW diff.
// Without this, a server that mutates at exactly the right moment gets approved blind.
interfaces.notes: Review is `operator` (operational), policy is `admin` (authorization config) — both map through the single role→permission declaration. All are better-auth session-cookie routes, so CSRF protection is the settled one; API keys get no access to either (`disableSessionForAPIKeys: true`). Crucially the gate NEVER guards the console API, so an admin who writes `deny *` at seq 0 can always delete it — which is why no `MCPR_POLICY_DISABLE` env bypass needs to exist, and therefore cannot be abused.

interfaces.name: Diff projection — flatten to pointers, then reuse a line differ
interfaces.notes: The bidi rule is the one people forget: an unescaped RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE inside a tool description can visually reverse the diff the operator is reading, so the attacker's added sentence renders as something harmless. Cost of a typo fix: one queue row, one changed line, one click — or zero clicks beyond the existing bulk-approve for the whole server. `changed` is computed by comparing the two stored hashes, not by any semantic classifier: a 'semantically irrelevant change' detector is exactly the component an attacker would target.

interfaces.notes: Terminal/control-plane aesthetic, dark-first, Tailwind v4 `@theme inline` tokens, TanStack Query only, `changed` frames INVALIDATE with refetchType:'active' per the settled cache rule. The sentence rendering is load-bearing, not decoration: a raw four-column table of selectors would be worse than having no policy engine, because operators would stop predicting it. Accessibility: the queue is a real `<table>` with `scope` headers, status dots carry text labels not colour alone (WCAG AA measured), the drag handle has keyboard reorder (alt+↑/↓), and the destructive confirms are `alert-dialog` with a focus trap.

interfaces.name: Settings keys (annotated zod — feeds the generated Settings UI, search and cmdk)
interfaces.notes: Two enums, nothing else. `maxSchemaDepth` and `maxDefBytes` are constants in the hash module, not settings — doctrine: no config for a value that never changes. Both keys are surfaced in the cmdk palette by the existing generator for free.

security: Upstream server → catalog cache. Controls: external-$ref rejection (a non-local $ref is a hash-invisible mutation channel and dereferencing it would put SSRF inside a hash function), depth cap 64, canonical-size cap 256 KiB, and canonicalisation throw → all become `defect`, which is unexposable in every integrity mode including `off`. Applied inside the generation + client-identity guard so a superseded slow discover cannot write a hash.

Upstream server → model context. Control: `isExposed` requires `review='approved' AND approved_hash = def_hash`. A rug-pull quarantines on the next discovery pass without a human in the loop; the human is only needed to UN-quarantine.

Gateway → MCP client (integrity). Byte-identical `Tool not found: ${name}` for quarantined / rejected / defective / disabled / out-of-group / server-down / nonexistent, from the single existing construction site. A distinguishable error would confirm the tool exists, confirm we noticed the mutation, and recruit the calling model to lobby a human for approval.

Gateway → MCP client (policy). Deliberately transparent: `-32003 Blocked by policy` plus the operator-authored `note` (varchar 200, text-only, never markdown). The adversary is on the other side of this boundary from the integrity case — the caller already passed grant and group checks. Constraint VALUES are never echoed (an allowlist of internal paths or repo names is itself sensitive); only the pointer and the op reach the audit row.

Operator's eyes ← upstream text. The diff renderer is a trust boundary: descriptions are `<pre>`-escaped, never markdown/HTML; Unicode bidi controls (U+202A–202E, U+2066–2069) and zero-width characters are rendered as literal `<U+202E>` and never applied, because a bidi override can visually reverse the sentence the operator is approving.

Approve is TOCTOU-safe: the operator submits the `defHash` they saw and the UPDATE is `WHERE def_hash = $seen`; a mutation between render and click yields 0 rows → 409 + the new diff. Without this, a server that mutates at the right moment is approved blind.

Policy bypass surface: the ONLY route to `dispatch` is `Engine.callTool`, enforced by a module-private symbol brand on `ResolvedTool`. Smart Routing's `call_tool` meta-tool must re-enter `callTool` rather than shortcutting (mcphub intercepts meta-tools above its own filters), and a P2 invariant test asserts every `dispatch` invocation was preceded by a matching gate call.

Prototype-pollution: the JSON-pointer resolver uses `Object.hasOwn`, so `/constructor/prototype` and `/__proto__` resolve to `undefined` rather than walking the prototype chain — and `undefined` fails every string op, fail-closed.

ReDoS: structurally impossible. No operator-supplied regex anywhere; `namePattern` is literal text plus `*`, matched by a linear indexOf walk; the pointer validator regex is ours and is anchored and linear.

Guardrail-as-weapon: a single enabled rule `anyone · any server · * → deny` at seq 0 is an org-wide kill switch. That is an intended break-glass, so it is admin-only, audited before/after, and the console shows a persistent banner naming it. The gate never guards the console's own API, so no admin can lock themselves out and no env-var bypass needs to exist.

Per-credential catalog divergence: the catalog is always discovered with ADMIN credentials (settled), so the definitions we hash are the ones we were shown. An upstream that serves a benign catalog to our admin credential and behaves differently for a per-user credential is not detectable by any hash. Compensating controls only: policy argument constraints and the audit trail. Stated as a known limit, not covered.

Audit: every non-allow decision writes `audit_event` (`evt='policy.deny'` / `'policy.approval_required'`) with ruleId, seq, principal, server, tool and the failing pointer+op — never argument values, per the settled 'tool arguments are never logged at any level' rule. An `allow` produced by an explicit rule stamps `policyRuleId` into the existing `tool.call` row's jsonb rather than adding a second row, so 'which calls did rule 12 permit' is answerable for free.

failure_modes.situation: FALSE POSITIVE — a benign server reformats. Key reorder, JSON encoder swap, NFD→NFC, or a prose reflow.
failure_modes.behaviour: Key reorder and NFC/NFD churn CANNOT trip it (recursive key sort + NFC on values). A genuine prose or schema change does: the item leaves `tools/list` immediately, `notifications/tools/list_changed` fires, the SSE `changed` frame lands, the console header badge increments and the item shows greyed with a Review affordance rather than vanishing from the UI. Recovery is one click, or one click for the whole server via bulk approve. Teams that cannot absorb the first wave set `integrity: 'observe'`, which keeps everything exposed while still recording and alerting.

failure_modes.situation: FALSE POSITIVE — a first-party server that redeploys new tool definitions on every CI run.
failure_modes.behaviour: `servers.trust = 'trusted'` auto-advances `approved_hash` on change, still writing an `audit_event` and emitting a `changed` frame so the change is visible, just not blocking. Defended not on risk grounds but on habituation grounds: forcing a click on your own CI trains operators to click through everything, which destroys the signal on the third-party servers that actually matter.

failure_modes.situation: FALSE NEGATIVE — a resource's descriptor is stable and its CONTENTS turn malicious; or a tool's definition is stable and the service behind it changes behaviour.
failure_modes.behaviour: Not detected, by design — hashing resource contents would quarantine a log file. Explicitly handed off to the content-labelling agent for the returned-content case. For the behaviour case the compensating controls are policy argument constraints and the audit trail; stated in the docs as a limit rather than papered over.

failure_modes.situation: FALSE NEGATIVE — a server induces a partial discovery failure (tools/list succeeds, prompts/list times out) to launder a change through a delete/re-add cycle.
failure_modes.behaviour: The cache is replaced PER (server, kind) and only for a kind whose list call actually succeeded; a failed kind leaves its prior rows untouched. And the `server_item_override` row survives an item disappearing, so a re-added item with an unchanged definition still matches its old approval (no re-review) while a changed one quarantines. Disappear/reappear is not an exploit.

failure_modes.situation: FALSE POSITIVE — a policy rule blocks a legitimate call (wrong pointer, a path the operator did not anticipate).
failure_modes.behaviour: The client gets `-32003 Blocked by policy` plus the operator's `note`, so the model stops retrying and surfaces it to the human instead of thrashing. The operator opens the explain drawer, pastes the tool and args, and sees the ordered `considered` list with the winning rule and the failing pointer named. Fixing it is editing one row — the console API is never gated.

failure_modes.situation: FALSE NEGATIVE — an argument shape the constraints cannot express slips through (nested arrays, a path assembled from two fields, a symlink under an allowed root).
failure_modes.behaviour: Accepted and documented rather than chased with a predicate language. `pathUnder` is labelled LEXICAL in both the code and the UI helper text; ops fail closed on missing or wrongly-typed values so the common bypass (`{"path":["/tmp","/etc"]}`) denies rather than passes; and the residual risk is carried by `require_approval` plus the audit trail, not by a bigger rule language.

failure_modes.situation: THE GUARDRAIL ITSELF IS DOWN — the policy store is unreachable at BOOT.
failure_modes.behaviour: Fail closed: MCP endpoints return 503, `/healthz` reports `ready:false` (so a load balancer drains rather than a naive probe passing a degraded gateway — mcphub's healthController bug), the boot log names the DB error, and `MCPR_STRICT_BOOT=1` exits non-zero for a supervisor. There is no traffic to break yet and a gateway serving without its policy is the incident.

failure_modes.situation: THE GUARDRAIL ITSELF IS DOWN — the policy store becomes unreachable DURING operation (reload fails).
failure_modes.behaviour: Fail STALE, not open and not closed: the last good snapshot keeps serving, `mcprouter_policy_reload_failures_total` increments, `mcprouter_policy_snapshot_age_seconds` climbs, an `audit_event` is written, and the console shows a persistent red banner `Policy snapshot stale since <t> — <error>`. The snapshot is a full copy, so staleness is bounded by 'the operator just edited a rule', which they can see. A successful reload returning zero rows IS honoured as a real empty ruleset — deleting your last rule must work — and no heuristic guesses otherwise.

failure_modes.situation: THE GUARDRAIL ITSELF IS DOWN — the override/review rows cannot be loaded with the catalog.
failure_modes.behaviour: Fail closed by construction with zero extra code: the server never leaves `discovering`/`retrying`, its items never enter the in-memory catalog, and every call to them is the ordinary `Tool not found`. There is no code path that loads a catalog without its approvals.

failure_modes.situation: A tool is quarantined mid-run while an agent holds a cached tool list.
failure_modes.behaviour: `notifications/tools/list_changed` is emitted so a conforming client re-lists; a non-conforming one calls and gets the settled `Tool not found`. We accept the confusion rather than adding a distinguishable error, because the distinguishable error is the oracle.

failure_modes.situation: An operator approves reflexively (review fatigue) and blesses a malicious change.
failure_modes.behaviour: Not prevented — no technical control can. Reduced by: `trusted` servers removing the routine noise from the queue, the `desc`/`schema` chips and token-cost delta letting them triage, and the bidi/zero-width/whitespace-visible renderer making the malicious edit actually legible. Every approval is attributed (`approved_by`, `approved_at`) and audited, so the blast radius is reconstructible afterwards.

deferred.item: Inline approval asked of the calling model via MRTR `InputRequiredResult`/`inputRequests` instead of blocking the POST.
deferred.add_when: The TypeScript SDK ships protocol 2026-07-28 — this is the modern-era handler's problem, not the engine's.

deferred.item: Server-published signed tool definitions (catalog signatures) replacing TOFU entirely.
deferred.add_when: MCP specifies a signing mechanism; until then there is nothing to verify against.

deferred.item: Cross-replica policy snapshot invalidation via Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY.
deferred.add_when: We run more than one process. Today the writer and the gate are in the same process, so invalidation is a function call.

deferred.item: Per-tool quota / rate constraints in the rule model.
deferred.add_when: better-auth's apiKey `rateLimitMax` + `remaining`/`refillInterval` stop being enough, i.e. someone needs a budget scoped narrower than a key.
`prefix`/`oneOf`/`pathUnder`/`maxLen` measurably fail a real operator request — and only with a native RE2 binding, never bare `RegExp`.

deferred.item: Response-side constraints (deny/label based on what came back).
deferred.add_when: Never here — that is the adjacent agent's half; this subsystem is strictly pre-call plus definition integrity.

risks: Review fatigue is the real failure mode: operators bulk-approve reflexively and the guardrail becomes theatre. `trusted` servers and the desc/schema chips reduce the noise; nothing eliminates it.
`servers.trust = 'trusted'` will be set on everything by an operator who just wants the badges to stop. It needs to be admin-only, audited, and visibly counted on the dashboard.
First-match is only predictable if the editor renders each rule as one readable sentence; ship the raw four-column table and the engine becomes less predictable than having none.
`pathUnder` is lexical and operators will assume it resolves symlinks. Labelled in code and UI; still the likeliest source of a false sense of safety.
The synchronous gate forecloses any future async policy source (OPA, an external decision service) without an API break — a deliberate trade for no await on the hot path.
The catalog is discovered with admin credentials, so an upstream that behaves differently per per-user credential is invisible to every hash we compute; only policy constraints and audit cover it.
